Q21198: Computer science studies how information can be represented and processed to solve problems. An algorithm turns inputs into outputs through defined steps. Comparing different procedures for the same task reveals why a correct solution can still be inefficient.
local:catalog:ephemeron: An ephemeron pairs a key with a value during garbage collection. The value is retained only when the key is reachable without depending on that value. A value’s reference back to its key therefore cannot, by itself, keep the pair alive.
local:catalog:hazard-pointer: A hazard pointer lets a thread announce that it is protecting an object in concurrent memory. Removed objects are retired before reclamation. Checking published hazard pointers delays freeing protected objects, separating removal from safe reuse of their memory.
local:catalog:epoch-based-memory-reclama: Epoch-based reclamation delays freeing objects removed from a concurrent structure. Readers pin the current epoch while accessing it. Retired objects wait until readers that could still hold references have finished, separating logical removal from safe memory reuse.
local:catalog:qpack-field-compression: QPACK compresses HTTP/3 field sections using a shared dynamic table and separate instruction streams. Referring to a table entry that has not arrived can block decoding. Limiting blocked streams trades compression reuse against the cost of waiting.
local:catalog:http-structured-field-dict: An HTTP Structured Fields dictionary is an ordered collection of unique textual keys and typed values. Values may be individual items or inner lists. A field specification gives those keys meaning, letting a common parser handle the representation.
local:catalog:http-message-signatures: HTTP Message Signatures authenticate selected request or response components and accompanying signature metadata. The signer builds a defined signature base from those covered parts. Verification therefore concerns the named coverage; it does not automatically authenticate every field or every message byte.
local:catalog:oblivious-http: Oblivious HTTP sends encrypted requests through a relay to a gateway. The relay sees the client but cannot read the request; the gateway decrypts it but sees the relay. Privacy depends on separated knowledge, including those parties not colluding.
local:catalog:merkle-inclusion-proof: A Merkle inclusion proof supplies the sibling hashes needed to recompute a tree’s root from one leaf. Matching an authenticated root establishes that leaf’s membership under the hash assumptions. It proves inclusion, rather than preservation of the entire earlier tree.
local:catalog:merkle-consistency-proof: A Merkle consistency proof connects an earlier tree root to a larger tree root through intermediate hashes. It establishes that the earlier leaves remain an unchanged prefix, supporting append-only history. This checks continuity between trees rather than one leaf’s membership.
Q65123731: In Gale–Shapley deferred acceptance, each proposer approaches their best remaining choice. Each recipient provisionally retains the preferred proposal and rejects others. With strict rankings in the standard one-to-one model, these repeated rounds yield a stable matching.
local:catalog:rural-hospitals-theorem: With fixed quotas, strict preferences and responsive hospital rankings, stable hospital–doctor matchings fill the same number of places at each hospital. The rural hospitals theorem also fixes which doctors an undersubscribed hospital receives, even when other assignments change.
local:catalog:top-trading-cycles: In school-choice top trading cycles, students point to preferred schools and schools point to remaining students with highest priority. Directed cycles assign seats; assigned students leave and capacities adjust. With strict rankings, repeating this process turns cycles into allocations.
local:catalog:boston-immediate-acceptanc: In the Boston school-choice mechanism described in 2003, schools fill seats permanently in rounds of first choices, then second choices and so on. Later applicants cannot displace earlier admissions through higher priority. Consequently, reporting true preferences is not generally a dominant strategy.
local:catalog:clarke-pivot-rule: In a quasilinear VCG mechanism, Clarke pivot payments compare others’ welfare in the chosen allocation with the best welfare they could obtain without that participant. The resulting transfer prices an imposed externality, tying payment to effects on others rather than the participant’s own valuation.
local:catalog:moral-hazard-in-teams: Moral hazard in teams arises when individual actions are hidden but joint output is observable. In Holmström’s model, sharing that output under a balanced budget can leave members with incentives to free ride. The team setting changes the contract-design problem.
local:catalog:relative-performance-evalu: Relative performance evaluation lets a contract use peers’ outcomes alongside an agent’s own performance. In Holmström’s model, comparing agents can provide information useful for incentives. The value of competition therefore depends on its informational role in the contracting problem.
local:catalog:multitask-incentive-proble: A multitask incentive model treats effort as attention allocated across different duties. When duties compete for that attention, rewarding easily measured output can divert effort from valuable work that is harder to measure. The effect depends on task substitution and measurement.
local:catalog:market-unraveling: In matching-market unraveling, participants arrange appointments progressively earlier to get ahead of competitors. Contracts can be signed before candidates’ qualifications or employers’ needs are clear. Roth and Xing’s historical examples show how this timing race can thin later opportunities.
local:catalog:runway-incursion: A runway incursion is an incorrect presence of an aircraft, vehicle or person in the protected area of a surface designated for aircraft landing and takeoff. The FAA safety category describes an occurrence, including cases without immediate collision consequences.
local:catalog:saturation-flow-rate: Saturation flow rate describes the hourly rate at which a queued lane could discharge under continuous green with no lost time. It is a reference flow: an actual signal cycle allocates only some of its time to effective green.
local:catalog:dutch-roll: Dutch roll is a coupled oscillation in an aircraft’s rolling and yawing motion. Depending on its lateral and directional stability, the motion may be weakly damped. Some aircraft use a yaw damper to reduce this recurring side-to-side motion.
local:catalog:p-factor: P-factor is asymmetric propeller loading at a high angle of attack. The blades experience unequal relative airflow, shifting the effective center of thrust away from the shaft. This creates a yawing tendency whose direction depends on propeller rotation.
local:catalog:adverse-yaw: When an aileron increases lift on one wing, it can also increase that wing’s drag. This differential drag can yaw the aircraft opposite to the intended bank. Adverse yaw therefore couples a roll-control input with an unwanted directional response.
local:catalog:etcs-braking-curve: ETCS braking curves predict how a train’s speed should change with distance toward a restriction. The calculation combines train braking characteristics with track data. These curves support speed supervision; their predicted trajectory is a model, not an exact realized stopping distance.
local:catalog:airport-surface-hotspot: An FAA airport hotspot is a movement-area location with a history or potential risk of collision or runway incursion. Identifying it directs pilots and vehicle drivers to pay heightened attention there. The designation concerns a risky location rather than a particular incident.
local:catalog:start-up-lost-time: When a traffic signal turns green, the first queued drivers need time to react and accelerate. Their initially longer discharge headways create start-up lost time before steady flow begins. This reduces the green time available for discharge at the saturation rate.
local:catalog:bus-queue-jump: A bus queue jump combines a short lane with a signal arrangement that gives the bus an early green. The bus can pass waiting traffic and rejoin the route ahead of the queue. The treatment links street geometry with signal timing.
Q11023: Engineering turns a practical problem into a design that can be tested. Designers set goals and constraints, build a prototype, compare its behavior with those goals, and revise it. A classroom rover challenge makes this cycle visible.
local:catalog:stableford-scoring: In Stableford golf, each hole earns points according to the player’s score relative to a fixed target. Those points, rather than the total number of strokes, are added across the round. The player with the most points wins.
local:catalog:maximum-score-golf: In Maximum Score golf, the committee sets a cap on the score for each hole. A player who does not finish the hole still receives that capped score. The format remains stroke play while bounding the contribution of a difficult hole.
local:catalog:libero-volleyball: Under FIVB 2025–2028 rules, the Libero replaces back-row players through special replacement procedures. The role cannot serve or block, and cannot complete an attack when the ball is entirely above the net at contact. Defensive specialization therefore comes with defined playing restrictions.
local:catalog:volleyball-rotational-faul: A rotational fault occurs when a volleyball team serves out of order. Under FIVB 2025–2028 rules, the order must be corrected and the opponent receives a point and next serve. The faulty team’s subsequent points are cancelled only if the fault’s start can be determined.
local:catalog:tennis-service-let: Under standard ITF rules, a serve that touches the net and is otherwise valid is a service let. That particular serve is repeated. If it was a second serve, an earlier first-service fault remains; the let does not restart the whole service sequence.
local:catalog:wheelchair-tennis-two-boun: Wheelchair tennis permits a player to return the ball after a second bounce. The first bounce must still satisfy the ordinary court-boundary rule; the second may land outside the court. The adaptation changes return timing while preserving the first-bounce requirement.
local:catalog:rugby-union-advantage: Rugby union advantage allows play to continue after an infringement when the non-offending team gains clear tactical or territorial benefit. A mere opportunity is insufficient. Subject to the law’s exceptions, the referee can return to the original infringement when no advantage materializes.
local:catalog:duckworth-lewis-stern-meth: The Duckworth–Lewis–Stern method adjusts targets in interrupted limited-overs cricket. ICC uses a Stern Edition calculator; its published Standard Edition fallback explains resources through overs remaining and wickets lost. Edition matters when interpreting the published target-adjustment methodology.
Q11413: Go is a two-player board game in which adjacent stones of one color share empty neighboring intersections called liberties. Losing every liberty captures the connected group. Under the territory-scoring rules in this guide, enclosed territory and prisoners contribute to the score.
local:catalog:voice-onset-time: Voice onset time measures the timing between a stop consonant’s release and the start of vocal-fold vibration. Voicing that begins before release gives a negative value. This timing dimension helps distinguish speech sounds without requiring one universal boundary between phonemes.
local:catalog:mcgurk-effect: The McGurk effect occurs when conflicting heard and seen speech can produce a perceived syllable present in neither input. Auditory ba paired with visual ga can be heard as da. Responses vary across listeners and stimuli, showing variability in audiovisual speech integration.
local:catalog:mutual-exclusivity-word-le: Mutual exclusivity is a word-learning default that discourages assigning an unfamiliar label to an already named whole object. It can guide a learner toward an unnamed object or property. Context can override the assumption; objects may legitimately have multiple names.
local:catalog:whole-object-assumption: The whole-object assumption is an initial hypothesis in word learning: a new label for an object names the object as a whole. It narrows possible meanings among parts, substances and properties, but other linguistic and contextual cues can override it.
local:catalog:generation-effect: Generating a word from a cue can leave a stronger memory than reading it. The generation effect emerged in experiments comparing those encoding conditions, with advantages in later recognition and recall. Its size and occurrence depend on the study conditions.
local:catalog:productive-failure: In Kapur’s 2006 study, student groups initially struggled with ill-structured problems without scaffolding. They later performed better on individual problems, including transfer, than a scaffolded comparison group. The result concerns that staged task design; unsuccessful exploration alone is not a general recipe.
local:catalog:desirable-difficulties: Desirable difficulties are learning conditions that can make practice feel harder while improving later retention or transfer. Their value depends on the learner being able to overcome them. Immediate fluency therefore gives an incomplete picture of lasting learning.
Q7705913: The testing effect is improved later retention following an earlier attempt to retrieve studied material. In prose-learning experiments, initial tests could produce better delayed recall than additional reading. Retrieval therefore can serve as a learning event as well as a measure of learning.
local:catalog:event-segmentation-theory: Event Segmentation Theory proposes that people use ongoing models to predict what happens next. A temporary rise in prediction error signals an event boundary and updates processing. The account connects perceived divisions in continuous activity with attention and memory.
local:catalog:change-blindness: Change blindness is failure to notice a change across successive views of a scene. A brief interruption, such as a blink or blank image, can let a substantial alteration escape detection. The phenomenon exposes limits in comparing scene information over time.
local:catalog:choice-blindness: In a choice-blindness experiment, participants selected a face and were sometimes shown the other face as their choice. Some failed to detect the switch and explained the presented outcome. The task reveals a possible gap between choosing and reporting reasons.
local:catalog:illusion-of-explanatory-de: The illusion of explanatory depth occurs when a feeling of understanding exceeds one’s ability to explain a mechanism. Attempting a detailed explanation can expose gaps and lower confidence. In the experiments, this gap was especially apparent for explanatory understanding.
local:catalog:stop-signal-reaction-time: Stop-signal reaction time estimates the latency of an unobserved stopping process. A race model relates ordinary response times and stop-signal delays to successful stopping. The estimate depends on the model and task behavior; deliberate slowing of go responses can distort interpretation.
local:catalog:simon-effect: In a Simon task, a stimulus’s color or shape determines the required response while its location is irrelevant. Responses are often faster when stimulus and response occur on corresponding sides. The Simon effect shows that irrelevant spatial information can influence action selection.
local:catalog:duration-neglect: Duration neglect describes evaluations that give an experience’s length little weight even when its duration is known. Fredrickson and Kahneman studied brief affective episodes; remembered evaluations did not simply track elapsed time. Their finding does not automatically extend to experiences lasting months.
local:catalog:inattentional-blindness: Inattentional blindness occurs when an unexpected visible event escapes awareness while attention is directed elsewhere. In Simons and Chabris’s counting task, some observers missed a conspicuous person crossing the scene. Detection varied with what observers attended to.
local:catalog:homophily: Homophily is the tendency for social ties to connect similar people. Shared traits can shape who meets whom and who forms a friendship. It describes a population pattern, allowing many individual ties between unlike people.
local:catalog:focal-closure: Focal closure occurs when two people sharing an activity or organization form a social tie. The shared focus supplies a setting for contact. In a social-affiliation network, the resulting edge connects people.
local:catalog:membership-closure: Membership closure occurs when someone joins an activity or organization through a friend’s existing affiliation. The added edge connects person and focus. In a social-affiliation network, existing friendships can therefore help shape new memberships.
local:catalog:complex-contagion: A complex contagion requires reinforcement from multiple contacts before adoption. In formal network models, an isolated long tie may carry information without supplying enough reinforcement. Several connected contacts can therefore matter for spreading these behaviors through a network.
local:catalog:friendship-paradox: The friendship paradox reflects sampling through social ties. People with many friends appear in more people’s friend lists, so they are overrepresented among friends. Average friend counts can consequently be higher in this sample; the statement concerns sampling rather than every individual.
local:catalog:preferential-attachment: Preferential attachment is a rule in which well-connected nodes are more likely to receive new links. Repeated growth can amplify an initial advantage, producing a few highly connected nodes. This is a simplified network model, not a universal explanation of popularity.
local:catalog:schelling-segregation-mode: In Schelling’s simplified two-group models, people move when local neighbors fail their tolerance threshold. Each move changes nearby composition, potentially prompting further moves and producing clusters. The result illustrates a collective pattern without treating real segregation as a single-cause process.
